ca_lone_rock.blurb: Lone Rock is a roughly 200-foot spire standing alone in a remote valley of northeastern California, in the Susanville area and far from any town. Of its 15 routes, twelve are trad and three are sport. The grades run from easy fifth class up to 5.12, but most of the climbs sit around 5.10, with little in between. The stone is rough and featured, and its faces point in several directions, so you can chase sun or shade. It is exposed to wind and temperature swings, and very quiet, which suits adventurous parties who want solitude more than a polished crag.

ca_hungover_wall_left_side.blurb: The left half of the Hungover Wall, a long and slightly overhanging crag high on Keller Peak in the San Bernardino Mountains above Running Springs. Fifteen routes here, twelve sport and three trad, run from 5.9 up to the low 5.13s, with the bulk between 5.10 and 5.12. The line starts at one end near the 5.10a Shiver Shot and runs along the base to the 5.11d Barfly. Expect technical, sustained moves on sharp crimps and seams. It was a pioneering summer sport crag for Southern California and often has few other parties around, even on weekends.
ca_hungover_wall_left_side.parking_note: The wall is 3.4 miles up Keller Peak Road, on the north side of the road. A pullout holds four or five cars, and there is more room a little farther up the road.
ca_hungover_wall_left_side.approach: The base is a one to two minute walk from the roadside parking.

ca_london_wall.blurb: London Wall is a sport-only wall in the Williamson Rock complex of the Angeles National Forest, off the Angeles Crest Highway in the San Gabriel Mountains. It sits a short way downstream from the Mushroom Boulder and just right of Stream Wall, with a seasonal creek running along its base. The 15 routes are all bolted and mostly hard: eight around 5.12, five at 5.11, and two at 5.10. Lines are long, sustained and powerful, rewarding good technique and core strength, and the best of them tend to draw queues. Not a place for beginners.

ca_main_wall_20.blurb: The Main Wall at Dry Falls is a granite crag in the San Jacinto Mountains above Palm Springs. It holds 15 routes, ten sport and five trad, running from about 5.6 to 5.11, with the largest cluster at 5.10. Some lines are a single pitch while others stretch to two or four pitches, so it suits a mix of short sport days and longer trad outings. The slabs face south and get strong sun, which makes early or late hours the comfortable times to be on them in warm weather.

ca_pinch_me_wall.blurb: Pinch Me Wall is one of the main crags at Land of the Lost, a cluster of quartzite crags on Horse Mountain in the forest east of Arcata and Eureka, near Willow Creek. It is the go-to wall for moderates: of its 15 routes, twelve are sport and three trad, spanning 5.5 to 5.12 with most climbs between 5.7 and 5.10. Lines run about 50 to 95 feet and are generally well bolted, though a few are close together. The friction on the stone is good, and the wall also offers gear placements for trad leaders. Camping is available near the main parking area.

ca_grain_central_station.blurb: Grain Central Station is a small cluster of rocks and boulders in Indian Cove, on the north side of Joshua Tree National Park, near the group campsites. It holds 15 routes, mostly trad with a couple of sport lines and one top rope. Grades run from easy scrambling to about 5.10, and most are 5.8 or below, so it works well for newer leaders and anyone seeking easier mileage. The rock is grainy and rough, hence the area names, and the surroundings are open desert with cactus. Shade is decent through much of the day.
